interview_metadata.name: Balbir Kakarala
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born and raised in New York, in a South Asian immigrant family. My dad comes from a Punjabi Sikh background and my mom is Telugu, so our home was this mix of languages, food, holidays, and expectations. Education was a big deal, but so were community and keeping some connection to India. I grew up around Diwali, Vaisakhi, Sankranti, temple or gurdwara visits now and then, and a lot of family friends who were basically aunties and uncles. I was a pretty quiet kid, more observant than loud, and I liked figuring things out. In school I leaned toward science and technology, but I was also the person who liked helping classmates understand things. In college I got a bachelor's degree and slowly realized I did not want to be only technical; I liked the part where you translate complicated material into something people can actually use. That led me toward training and instructional design. Now I live in Brooklyn, work as a training and development specialist, and spend my time building e-learning modules, running needs assessments, and working with subject-matter experts. Personally, I have never been married and I do not have children. My life is pretty steady: work, cooking, jogging in Prospect Park, board games with friends, volunteering as a STEM tutor, and trying to grow into a senior learning-and-development role.

follow_ups.question: What are some specific childhood memories that still shape how you live now?
follow_ups.response: Food is probably the clearest one. My mom making dal with coriander and turmeric, my dad insisting we help clean before guests came, and everyone sitting around after dinner talking over chai. I still cook lentils, rice, and flatbreads when I want to feel grounded.

follow_ups.question: Who were the main people around you growing up?
follow_ups.response: My parents were the center of it, and I had relatives and family friends in the broader South Asian community. I also had school friends from different backgrounds, which felt normal in New York. That mix made me comfortable moving between cultures.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The main crossroads was near the end of college. I had enough STEM coursework that I could have gone toward a more technical analyst path, maybe data or operations. At the same time, I had been tutoring and helping design training materials for student groups, and I noticed I enjoyed the human side of learning more than sitting alone with technical tasks all day. I remember working on a workshop where students who were anxious about a software tool finally relaxed because the instructions were clearer. That felt meaningful. I chose to look for training and learning-design roles instead of trying to force myself into a more conventional technical track. It changed how I saw myself: not as someone leaving STEM, but as someone translating it.

follow_ups.question: Was there a particular person who influenced that choice?
follow_ups.response: A college advisor helped. She pointed out that instructional design was a real field, not just something people do on the side. That gave me language for what I already liked doing.

follow_ups.question: What did your family think about that decision?
follow_ups.response: They were supportive but a little confused at first. My parents understood teaching and technology separately, but learning and development as a corporate job took some explaining.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice, but not a dramatic one. I made a spreadsheet of possible roles, talked to a few people, and noticed I kept getting more energized by training work than by pure technical jobs.

follow_ups.question: What did you weigh most heavily?
follow_ups.response: Whether the work would feel useful day to day. I also cared about stability and a path to grow.

follow_ups.question: Did you ever second-guess it?
follow_ups.response: A little, especially when technical roles seemed to pay more early on. But I felt more like myself in learning design.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. More formal career guidance would have helped. I found instructional design mostly by piecing things together, and I think colleges could do better showing students hybrid career paths.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Informational interviews, examples of actual job descriptions, and someone explaining credentials like CPLP earlier.

follow_ups.question: Did you eventually find that kind of support?
follow_ups.response: Some of it through LinkedIn, coworkers, and professional webinars. It was just scattered.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am not married, I do not have children, and I am not currently living with a romantic partner. My parents are still very important to me. They do not live with me, but we talk often, usually a few times a week by phone or text. My dad can be practical and direct, and my mom is more emotionally tuned in, so I go to them for different things. I also have extended family I see around holidays or community events. Family is not in my apartment every day, but it is in the background of my routines: the food I cook, the languages I understand, the holidays I show up for, and the pressure I put on myself to keep moving forward.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually once or twice a month, depending on work and everyone's schedule. Holidays and birthdays are more fixed.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do when you get together?
follow_ups.response: A meal is almost always involved. Sometimes I bring something I cooked, and sometimes we just sit around and catch up about work, family news, and health.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is mainly my parents. I am close to some cousins, but they feel more like extended family than daily immediate family.

follow_ups.question: Do you have siblings?
follow_ups.response: No, I do not have siblings.

follow_ups.question: Are your cousins nearby?
follow_ups.response: A few are in the New York and New Jersey area, so I see them occasionally.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My close friends matter a lot. I have a small board-game group that meets every couple of weeks, usually four or five of us playing things like Terraforming Mars or cooperative strategy games. I also know people through Prospect Park Runners, though those relationships are more casual. At work I have a couple coworkers I trust and sometimes get coffee with. I am not in a serious romantic relationship right now.

follow_ups.question: Who do you spend the most social time with in a normal month?
follow_ups.response: Probably my board-game friends. We rotate apartments or meet at a cafe with enough table space.

follow_ups.question: How do you usually keep in touch with friends?
follow_ups.response: Mostly group chats, Instagram messages, and calendar invites when someone is organized enough to make one.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Brooklyn, in the 11211 area, so Williamsburg and the surrounding North Brooklyn feel like my everyday radius. It is busy, walkable, expensive, and full of food, coffee shops, small markets, and people who always seem to be carrying a laptop or a tote bag. I like being near transit and having access to parks and cultural things without needing a car. I also like that there are South Asian groceries not too far away if I plan ahead. The neighborhood can feel a little polished and pricey, but it is convenient.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often in the neighborhood?
follow_ups.response: Grocery stores, coffee shops, the subway, and sometimes the waterfront. For bigger runs I go to Prospect Park, even though that means traveling a bit.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: Only lightly. I know a couple people in the building by face and small talk, but it is not a very neighborly building.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I generally feel safe. I stay aware late at night, especially around subway platforms, but I do not feel afraid in my normal routines.

follow_ups.question: Are there times you feel less comfortable?
follow_ups.response: Very late nights, especially if I am coming back alone after an event.

follow_ups.question: Do you change your behavior because of that?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I take better-lit routes or rideshare if it is really late.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is access: food, transit, friends, culture, and work opportunities. The downside is rent, noise, and the feeling that every small errand costs more than it should.

follow_ups.question: What do you like most about it?
follow_ups.response: Being able to decide last minute to meet someone, see a show, or grab ingredients.

follow_ups.question: What frustrates you most?
follow_ups.response: Housing costs and the constant background noise.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live with one roommate in a rented Brooklyn apartment. We each have our own bedroom and share the kitchen, living area, and bathroom. We are friendly but not best friends; we coordinate bills, cleaning, and basic apartment stuff. No one else is staying with us right now.

follow_ups.question: How do you divide household chores?
follow_ups.response: Mostly informally. I clean the kitchen more because I cook more, and my roommate handles trash and some shared supplies.

follow_ups.question: Do you eat together?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, though I sometimes offer food if I make a big pot of dal or rice.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent member of the household right now.

follow_ups.question: Is your roommate on the lease?
follow_ups.response: Yes, we are both on the lease.

follow_ups.question: Any short-term guests at the moment?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Occasionally a friend crashes on the couch after board-game night, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Any family staying over regularly?
follow_ups.response: No, family visits are usually daytime.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one who usually lives here is away.

follow_ups.question: Has that happened recently?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is stable?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it is just the two of us.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are fairly structured. I usually wake up around 6:30 or 7, jog some mornings, make coffee, and start work around 9. Some days I am deep in course design, storyboards, or LMS reports; other days are full of meetings with managers and subject-matter experts. Evenings vary between cooking, reading, board games, or tutoring. Tuesdays and Saturdays I often connect with Prospect Park Runners, depending on weather and workload. Sundays are usually meal prep, laundry, and resetting my calendar.

follow_ups.question: What does a good weekday morning look like?
follow_ups.response: Up by 6:30, short meditation, coffee, maybe a run, then checking my project list before meetings start.

follow_ups.question: What tends to throw the routine off?
follow_ups.response: Late work revisions or saying yes to spontaneous plans.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work as a training and development specialist, basically an instructional designer with some facilitation and analytics mixed in. My normal schedule is Monday through Friday, roughly 9 to 5:30. I build e-learning modules in Articulate Storyline and sometimes Adobe Captivate, organize training content, review learner data, and coordinate with subject-matter experts. Some weeks are heavier when a rollout is close, but it is a standard full-time job.

follow_ups.question: Do you work remotely or in person?
follow_ups.response: Hybrid. I work from home some days and go in when we have planning sessions, trainings, or team meetings.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job takes the most time?
follow_ups.response: Revisions. Getting content from experts into clear learning modules always takes more cycles than people expect.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I volunteer as a STEM tutor for middle-school students, usually once a week when the program is running. I also try to meditate most mornings, even if it is just ten minutes. I cook several times a week because eating out gets expensive and I like having leftovers. I also keep a loose professional development routine: webinars, reading about learning analytics, and slowly preparing for the CPLP credential.

follow_ups.question: When do you tutor?
follow_ups.response: Usually one weekday evening, around 6 or 6:30, depending on the program schedule.

follow_ups.question: What do you cook most often?
follow_ups.response: Dal, rice pilaf, vegetable stir-fries with Indian spices, and sometimes fusion experiments like masala tacos.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: Recently I have tried to make my mornings more consistent. I used to let work messages pull me in immediately, but now I try to run or meditate before opening email. I also joined more regular runs with Prospect Park Runners, which gives my week some structure. On the other hand, work has had a few new training launches, so some evenings have been less predictable.

follow_ups.question: What prompted the morning change?
follow_ups.response: I noticed I was starting the day reactive and scattered. Running first makes me calmer.

follow_ups.question: Has it stuck?
follow_ups.response: Mostly. I am not perfect about it, but three or four mornings a week is realistic.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids.

follow_ups.question: Do children play any role in your weekly routine through family or volunteering?
follow_ups.response: Yes, through STEM tutoring. That is the main child-related responsibility in my week.

follow_ups.question: Do you see yourself having children someday?
follow_ups.response: Possibly, but it is not an immediate plan.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited. I have had ordinary interactions, like seeing police in subway stations or at big events, and I have never been arrested or seriously questioned. As a brown man in New York, I am aware of how quickly people can feel watched or misread, but I would not say I have had a traumatic personal experience with law enforcement.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever been stopped by police?
follow_ups.response: No, not in a formal stop.

follow_ups.question: How do police presence in the city make you feel?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. Sometimes it feels reassuring, sometimes it feels tense depending on the context.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Protests and subway incidents stand out more than personal encounters. Seeing police lines at demonstrations made me think more critically about crowd control and power.

follow_ups.question: Were you present at any protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one racial justice march in Brooklyn, but I stayed toward the edge.

follow_ups.question: Did anything happen there?
follow_ups.response: Nothing violent where I was, but the police presence was heavy.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No one in my immediate family has been arrested, and I have not been arrested. I have heard friends talk about minor tickets or protest-related scares, but nothing close to me like incarceration.

follow_ups.question: Has that shaped how you think about the justice system?
follow_ups.response: It means my view comes more from listening, reading, and seeing patterns than from direct family experience.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with friends?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially friends who have had more direct experiences.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote regularly, especially in presidential, congressional, and New York local elections. I have missed a small local race before, but I try not to. I usually read voter guides and ask friends about local candidates because city politics can be hard to track.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in primaries?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually Democratic primaries, because in New York those often matter a lot.

follow_ups.question: How do you decide on local candidates?
follow_ups.response: I look at housing, transit, education, and endorsements from groups I trust.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as progressive-leaning and generally Democratic, but I am more pragmatic than ideological. I care about public education, health care access, climate, transit, housing affordability, and racial justice. Because of my family background, immigrant rights and respect for religious and cultural minorities matter to me too. I also care about competence in government. I work in training, so I think a lot about whether institutions actually help people learn, adapt, and use services. I am skeptical of big slogans when the implementation is vague. In New York, housing is probably the issue I feel most personally because rent shapes so many life choices.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most immediate in your own life?
follow_ups.response: Housing affordability. Even with a decent job, rent makes long-term planning feel tight.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents share your politics?
follow_ups.response: Broadly, yes, though they are sometimes more cautious or moderate on specific social issues.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on implementation and local government. In my early twenties I thought mostly in national terms: presidents, Congress, big issues. Living in Brooklyn and paying rent made zoning, transit, sanitation, and local budgeting feel much more concrete. I am still progressive, but I pay more attention to whether a proposal has a workable plan and who might be affected unintentionally.

follow_ups.question: Was there a specific event that shifted you?
follow_ups.response: The pandemic years and the housing market afterward. They made local capacity feel very real.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk politics often?
follow_ups.response: With some friends, yes. With family, yes, but carefully if it gets heated.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me a lot in terms of awareness and reflection. I am not Black, so I try not to center myself, but I do think being South Asian gives me some understanding of racialization and being perceived through stereotypes. Black Lives Matter pushed me to listen more carefully to Black friends and coworkers and to think about policing, schools, housing, and workplace equity as connected systems.

follow_ups.question: Did it change anything you did day to day?
follow_ups.response: It changed what I read and who I listened to. At work, it also made me more attentive to inclusive training design.

follow_ups.question: Did you discuss it with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially around anti-Blackness in immigrant communities. Those conversations were not always easy.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about them as institutional issues, not just individual prejudice. Policing is part of it, but so are schools, hiring, housing, and who gets treated as credible or threatening. I also think about how Asian and South Asian communities can sometimes want acceptance by distancing themselves from Black struggles, and that bothers me. I try to be honest about that without pretending I have all the answers.

follow_ups.question: What does being honest about that look like?
follow_ups.response: Calling out stereotypes in conversation, reading beyond headlines, and supporting policies that address structural inequity.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel hopeful about change?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I think awareness is higher, but institutions change slowly.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: Race feels impossible to separate from everyday systems. In New York you see incredible diversity, but also huge inequality across neighborhoods. I think a lot about the model minority stereotype and how it flattens Asian Americans while also being used against other groups. I have also been thinking about how workplace diversity efforts can become performative unless they change decision-making and promotion paths.

follow_ups.question: Does your own workplace address race well?
follow_ups.response: It tries, but unevenly. There are trainings and ERG conversations, but the real test is hiring and leadership.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify strongly as South Asian American?
follow_ups.response: Yes, definitely. It shapes how I move through these conversations.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and family, donated occasionally, attended one march, and tried to bring the learning into my work. I am not a constant activist, but I do not keep it completely private either.

follow_ups.question: What kind of organizations have you donated to?
follow_ups.response: Mostly local mutual aid or racial justice groups, not huge amounts but what I could.

follow_ups.question: How did the march feel?
follow_ups.response: Serious, emotional, and a little tense because of the police presence.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends mostly take it seriously, though people vary in how active they are. Some went to multiple protests, some donated, some mostly had conversations online. My parents are sympathetic but more cautious, partly because they worry about protests and conflict. In South Asian circles, I have seen both real solidarity and some defensiveness.

follow_ups.question: Have any conversations changed your relationships?
follow_ups.response: Not dramatically, but they showed me who is willing to sit with discomfort.

follow_ups.question: Do your board-game friends talk about politics?
follow_ups.response: Yes, usually before or after the game, not during the rules explanation.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall my health is good. I am not a serious athlete, but I jog regularly, usually in Prospect Park, and that keeps me in decent shape. I meditate, cook at home, and try to sleep enough, though work deadlines sometimes interfere. I do not have a major chronic condition that I know of.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Three or four times a week when I am consistent.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a regular doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I have a primary care doctor through my insurance.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Living in Brooklyn makes walking easy, and having Prospect Park as a running destination helps. Cooking also helps because I can control what I eat. The hard parts are stress, late meetings, winter weather, and the temptation to order food when I am tired.

follow_ups.question: What food do you order when tired?
follow_ups.response: Thai, pizza, or Indian takeout, depending on the night.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you accountable?
follow_ups.response: The running club helps because people expect you to show up.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing major. I had some knee soreness from increasing mileage too quickly, but rest, stretching, and better shoes helped. I also had a period of stress headaches during a busy work rollout. No major diagnosis, surgery, broken bones, or hospitalization.

follow_ups.question: Did you see a doctor for the knee soreness?
follow_ups.response: No, I managed it conservatively because it improved with rest.

follow_ups.question: Are the headaches still happening?
follow_ups.response: Not regularly. They mostly show up when I ignore sleep and hydration.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: My health has not seriously affected my ability to work. Stress can make me less focused, but I have not needed extended leave or anything like that.

follow_ups.question: Have you taken sick days recently?
follow_ups.response: A couple for colds or needing rest, but nothing major.

follow_ups.question: Do you adjust work when stressed?
follow_ups.response: I break tasks into smaller pieces and block focus time.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: It has come up in ordinary family ways. My parents are getting older, so I pay attention to their checkups, blood pressure, and whether they are taking care of themselves. Nothing catastrophic recently, but I feel that shift where I am starting to think about them as people who may need more support over time.

follow_ups.question: Do you help them with appointments?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I help interpret insurance paperwork or remind them to follow up.

follow_ups.question: Does that worry you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, quietly. It is not daily panic, but it is in the background.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have been lucky to have employer health insurance, so I have not had to forgo major care. The frustrating part is navigating networks, copays, and appointment availability. For mental health especially, finding someone affordable and available can be hard. For my parents, insurance paperwork can be confusing, so I sometimes help them compare bills or messages.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever delayed care because of cost?
follow_ups.response: I have delayed minor things, like physical therapy or dental follow-up, but not emergency care.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust your doctors?
follow_ups.response: Generally yes, though I still double-check information.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, mostly informal South Asian home remedies. Ginger tea, turmeric milk, ajwain for digestion, steam inhalation when congested, that kind of thing. My family may describe some of it as Ayurvedic, though we are not seeing an Ayurvedic practitioner regularly. I use those things for comfort, not as a replacement for medical care when something is serious.

follow_ups.question: Which remedy do you personally use most?
follow_ups.response: Ginger tea with honey when I feel a cold coming on.

follow_ups.question: Who taught you those remedies?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mom and older relatives.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, maybe a beer or cocktail with friends, but not as my main coping strategy. When I am stressed, I am more likely to run, cook, scroll too much, or watch something low-effort. I try to notice if I am using anything to avoid feelings.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: A few times a month, usually one or two drinks.

follow_ups.question: Any tobacco or vaping?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not rely on prescriptions, pain meds, marijuana, or other substances to cope. I have used over-the-counter ibuprofen for soreness or headaches. I have tried cannabis socially in the past, but it is not a regular part of my life. The most recent substance use was probably having a drink with friends, not anything stronger.

follow_ups.question: When did you last use marijuana?
follow_ups.response: Probably more than a year ago, socially, and not something I sought out.

follow_ups.question: Do you take any daily medications?
follow_ups.response: No daily prescriptions.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I use my employer insurance and pay copays or out-of-pocket costs as they come up. My parents have their own coverage, and I help them understand bills when needed. We are not in a crisis around health care costs, but everyone still watches expenses because even routine care can add up.

follow_ups.question: Do you budget for medical costs?
follow_ups.response: Loosely. I keep some savings for copays or unexpected bills.

follow_ups.question: Are prescriptions expensive for your family?
follow_ups.response: Not severely right now, but it depends on coverage.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am pro-vaccine. I got COVID vaccines and boosters as recommended, and I get the flu shot most years. I see vaccination as basic public health.

follow_ups.question: Did your family feel the same way?
follow_ups.response: Mostly yes, though there were normal questions about timing and side effects.

follow_ups.question: Any hesitation yourself?
follow_ups.response: Not really. I just wanted reliable information.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my doctor, the CDC, major hospital systems, and scientifically grounded reporting. I also listen to medically trained friends when they explain things clearly. I try not to rely on random social media posts, especially when they are designed to provoke fear.

follow_ups.question: Do you fact-check health information?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially if something sounds dramatic or too simple.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents ask you about vaccine information?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. They may send me an article and ask what I think.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: The past year has been mostly stable but mentally busy. I feel grateful for work and friends, but I also feel pressure about the future: career growth, rent, savings, whether I am moving fast enough. follow_ups.question: Was he usually employed steadily?

follow_ups.question: Did he work long hours?

transcript.question_text: What was his job? What kind of work did he do? What were his most important activities or duties?
transcript.response: My dad worked in information technology support. He helped maintain systems, troubleshoot technical problems, support users, and keep office technology running. He was practical and methodical, and I think I got some of my analytical habits from watching him.

follow_ups.question: Did he teach you about computers?
follow_ups.response: Yes, informally. He encouraged me to be comfortable with technology.

follow_ups.question: Was he a manager?
follow_ups.response: Not always formally, but he often handled responsibility and coordination.

transcript.question_text: What kind of place did he work for? What kind of business was it? What did they make or do where he worked?
transcript.response: He worked for office-based organizations that used IT systems to run their operations. The business itself was service-oriented, not manufacturing. His role was keeping the technology reliable so other people could do their jobs.

follow_ups.question: Was it in the private sector?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly private-sector office environments.

follow_ups.question: Did his job influence your career?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it made technology feel normal, but I took it toward learning and training.

transcript.question_text: We all have hopes about what our future will look like. Imagine yourself a few years from now. Maybe you want your life to be the same in some ways as it is now. Maybe you want it to be different in some ways. What do you hope for?
transcript.response: A few years from now, I hope to be in a senior learning-and-development role, maybe managing programs or mentoring junior designers. I want to earn the CPLP credential and become stronger in inclusive, data-driven training design. Personally, I hope to keep my friendships close, be more financially disciplined, and maybe have a clearer sense of whether I want to stay in New York long term. I also want to keep running, cooking, traveling on a reasonable budget, and showing up for my parents as they get older. I do not want a completely different life; I want this life to feel more intentional and less improvised.

follow_ups.question: What would success look like at work?
follow_ups.response: Owning larger learning programs that actually improve performance, not just producing modules.

follow_ups.question: What personal change would matter most?
follow_ups.response: Better financial consistency and less overthinking.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value family, learning, integrity, and being useful to other people. I also value quiet time, because I need space to think and reset. My background taught me respect for elders and community, but living in Brooklyn taught me openness and adaptability. At my best, I am trying to build a life where I can grow professionally without losing the small things that keep me grounded.

follow_ups.question: What small thing keeps you grounded most reliably?
follow_ups.response: Cooking a familiar meal, especially dal and rice.

follow_ups.question: What value guides your work?
follow_ups.response: Clarity. I like helping people understand what used to feel confusing.
